_why: ADR 0104's table. The title of the paper backing a value now reaches the

_why_three_files: Not just the new one. The change edits a string that THREE parsers read,
and the tests pinning those parsers live in the other two files. ADR
0026's set ran a narrower command on its first attempt and produced a
confident NOT CAUGHT because the test closing the mutation lived in the
second of the two files the record named.

If this is NOT caught, the new test is decoration.

mutations.description: the title is placed BEFORE the ref group, where the parsers read
_note: The real risk of this change, and the reason position is commented
as load-bearing. `/\(ref ([^)]*)\)/` reads the ref id out of the
first parenthesis; a title containing a bracket, or simply sitting
ahead of the group, moves what those three parsers see.
This mutation is what a well-meaning tidy-up would produce -- title
first reads more naturally -- and it must fail loudly rather than
quietly returning a wrong reference id.

_t3_withdrawn_and_why: T3 moved the locator gate below the title, so a citation with a name and
nothing to find it by would be admitted. It ran, and came back NOT
CAUGHT -- correctly, and the reason is a property of the code worth
recording rather than a gap worth filing.
A title-only citation produces no locators either, so the second gate
refuses it whatever the first one does. Mutating either alone changes no
observable behaviour, and mutating both would only prove that removing
all the protection removes the protection.
So the double gate is defence in depth that a mutation DEMONSTRATED
rather than assumed -- the same shape as ADR 0100's G2, which also could
not be expressed as a single mutation because the weakness was
conditional. Recording it as NOT CAUGHT would put a gap in this table
